lines: -Reinforcement learning for multi-turn LLM agents requires credit assignment across long interaction trajectories. The dominant training paradigm decomposes these trajectories into fixed-size windows optimized independently via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), yet this ubiquitous design choice has received little scrutiny. We identify a structural credit assignment pathology driven by two distinct mechanisms: \textit{policy information loss}, which truncates cross-window context and imposes a constant performance ceiling, and \textit{advantage sign misattribution}, which causes a substantial fraction of gradient updates for locally correct actions to carry incorrect sign. A partial factorial experiment (3 of 4 cells) isolates each mechanism: removing sign misattribution converts catastrophic collapse into bounded learning; removing information loss enables out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Direct sign measurement confirms the theoretical prediction, with credit agreement dropping to near-random levels. Episode-level GRPO, which treats the full trajectory as a single optimization sample, addresses both failure modes, yielding 17.2\% mean OOD success versus 6.7\% SFT baseline. However, a systematic multi-seed evaluation reveals that avoiding collapse is necessary but not sufficient: 73\% of seeds stabilize, yet only 36\% achieve statistically significant OOD transfer. Cross-scale verification at 8B parameters and cross-environment validation on ScienceWorld provide preliminary evidence that the pathology extends beyond our primary setting.

The credit assignment problem---determining which actions contributed to an outcome---is fundamental to RL~\cite{sutton1988td,williams1992reinforce}. Classical solutions include temporal difference learning, eligibility traces, and generalized advantage estimation~\cite{schulman2016gae} (Appendix~\ref{app:classical_connection}). Step-independent GRPO inherits the worst of outcome-vs-process supervision~\cite{lightman2024lets}: all windows receive episode-level credit regardless of individual action quality. Recent methods address this at different granularities: ArCHer~\cite{zhou2024archer} and VinePPO~\cite{kazemnejad2024vineppo} improve value estimation, PRIME~\cite{prime2025} and VAPO~\cite{vapo2025} refine credit granularity, while GiGPO~\cite{feng2025gigpo}, Turn-PPO~\cite{turnppo2025}, GAGPO~\cite{gagpo2026}, and HCAPO~\cite{hcapo2026} propose step- or turn-level advantage computation that preserves sign correctness. Our framework provides a unified explanation for \textit{why} these finer-grained methods succeed: they eliminate M2 (sign misattribution) while operating within the windowed framework.
